name: Ahithophel
bio:
Ahithophel the Gilonite was David's trusted counselor, renowned for advice so sound it was regarded "as if one consulted the word of God" (2 Samuel 16:23). When Absalom launched his rebellion, he sent for Ahithophel from his hometown of Giloh while the conspiracy was gathering strength, and Ahithophel's defection to Absalom's side was a severe blow — news of it reached David as he fled Jerusalem, prompting his anguished prayer, "LORD, turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness" (2 Samuel 15:12, 31).

Once in Jerusalem, Ahithophel advised Absalom to publicly sleep with his father's concubines, a deliberate, irreversible act meant to show all Israel that Absalom was now utterly estranged from David, strengthening the resolve of everyone who had joined the rebellion (2 Samuel 16:20-22). He then urged Absalom to let him pursue David immediately with twelve thousand men, striking while David was exhausted and demoralized and killing only the king himself, so the rest of the people could be brought back in peace — sound, decisive military advice that pleased Absalom and the elders of Israel (2 Samuel 17:1-4). But when Absalom also called for David's friend Hushai, planted inside his court as a spy, Hushai argued persuasively against striking so quickly, urging Absalom to gather all Israel for one massive campaign instead; Absalom and the elders judged Hushai's advice better than Ahithophel's, "for the LORD had determined to frustrate the good advice of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom" (2 Samuel 17:5-14).

Seeing that his counsel had been rejected, Ahithophel saddled his donkey and went home to his own city, set his affairs in order, and hanged himself, and was buried in his father's tomb (2 Samuel 17:23) — a stark end for a man whose wisdom had once seemed almost divine.
